entries.title: Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety
entries.summary: The three fired workers say OpenAI punished them for being outspoken about safety. The company disputes the claims and says they were fired over mishandling sensitive information.
entries.content:
Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology.

The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.

OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.

The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.

The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.

In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.

As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators, who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.

The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.

In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.

In a statement OpenAI posted on X, the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."

The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.

"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.

"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.

He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.

A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X, echoing Balesni's concerns.

The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.

In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.

Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.

Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.

"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."

OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.

OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.

In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.

"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

entries.title: Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
entries.summary: Trump says the U.S. will obtain diesel from Russia, relaxing years of U.S. pressure on Moscow, to combat prices before midterms. He said he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call.
entries.content:
Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.

Trump's announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.

Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."

Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.

Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday's news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.

A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."

Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."

The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement.

Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash

Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.

"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."

"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."

The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.

It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months

Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.

This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war.

The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year.

The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine.

Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine's repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is "immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule." He said that Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. already in October, and that Russia's domestic market will be "fully supplied" with diesel, as well.

entries.title: The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that
entries.summary: The Pentagon says it will livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan at Fort Hood, the site of his 2009 mass shooting. That would be the first public execution in the U.S. since the 1930s.
entries.content:
The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that

The Pentagon says it will livestream the planned military execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

Hasan, 56, has been on military death row since his conviction and sentencing in 2013. His case returned to the public spotlight this week when the Pentagon announced that President Trump had approved his death by firing squad — a first for the military since World War II.

The Pentagon says Hasan's execution will take place on the afternoon of Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the site of his shooting rampage. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the proceedings would be available for public viewing.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said in a video interview with Real America's Voice, a right-wing streaming network.

The Pentagon confirmed to NPR in a statement Friday that the execution "will be livestreamed," saying details would follow.

But much remains uncertain. Legal experts have said Hasan could delay his execution by years if he decides to file a habeas corpus appeal in federal court. Michael Radelet, a professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder who studies capital punishment, says outside groups could potentially challenge the livestream plans too.

"Hegseth is a rather controversial person," Radelet told NPR. "If he says, 'Do it this way,' it's not at all clear that it will actually be done that way."

If it does come to pass, it would be the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century — and the first ever to be livestreamed.

"Public executions have typically been held in authoritarian countries to instill fear in the population and to show the power and control of the government," Robin Maher, the executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told NPR. "We're not aware of any regulation or historical precedent for a [U.S.] military execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public."

The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was 90 years ago

The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was the hanging of Rainey Bethea — a Black man convicted of raping a white woman — in 1936. The case drew national attention.

Roughly 20,000 people gathered in the western Kentucky city of Owensboro, where workers had built a gallows near the riverfront, according to NPR station WKMS. People celebrated with "necktie" parties the night before and sipped soft drinks at the scene in what attendees and historians describe as a festive atmosphere.

"They sold sandwiches and they sold Coca-Colas, and you'd have thought it was a big picnic or something," attendee Bill Shelton recalled in a 2013 oral history interview with the Daviess County Public Library.

The spectacle prompted a public backlash over the perceived barbarity of executions. Kentucky held a "semipublic" hanging in a prison yard the following year, Radelet said, before outlawing public executions altogether in 1938. There haven't been any in the U.S. since.

He said the closest example was the lethal injection of Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001. The Justice Department made a closed-circuit telecast available for designated survivors and victims' loved ones to watch remotely; 232 of them gathered in a viewing room in Oklahoma City to do so.

"It's like getting rid of the guillotine — when it's gone, it's gone," Radelet said. "There was no serious discussion about bringing it back."

He said public executions fell out of favor for two main reasons: They are no longer widely believed to be a crime deterrent, and authorities became worried that public executions — especially those that went wrong — would turn people against the death penalty.

In fact, as part of that shift, executions have become less visible over time, Maher said. Initially, she said, states would conduct them in the middle of the night. Now, she said, some states that still carry out the death penalty have limited access for media witnesses.

"We moved away from public executions quite deliberately because they had turned into spectacles. That was not sitting comfortably with people anymore," said Maher. "And I think there was a move away from that sort of circus environment to inside prisons in the middle of the night."

Tennessee's recent botched lethal injection of Christa Pike has reignited debate over the death penalty. Radelet thinks a firing squad execution — especially if it's livestreamed — could further diminish public support for capital punishment, already at a five-decade low.

"There probably wouldn't be too much blood, but enough to make people talk about it over their morning coffee, if they're not sick," Radelet said. "And that discussion might be yet another step towards abolishing the death penalty."

Justin Mazzola, deputy research director at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement that Hegseth's announcement "adds to the display of cruelty" seen recently with Pike's botched execution.

"The U.S. death penalty is irredeemably broken," he said. "It is high time that the U.S. authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all."

Leaders call for Hegseth to reverse course

Hegseth's comments were met immediately with questions, concerns and calls for reconsideration. On Friday, Vice President Vance told reporters, "If it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, released a statement saying a public execution "will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

"In no way can Hassan's [sic] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he wrote.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., wrote on X that he supports Hasan's death sentence but called a livestream "beyond disgusting."

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," he wrote. "It should not be happening in America."

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, similarly mused on CNN about whether Hegseth is "mimicking ISIS executions." He called public executions "medieval" regardless of people's feelings about the death penalty itself.

The top Democrats on both the House and Senate Armed Services committees issued statements condemning the Pentagon's plan. Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, called it "another stunt by Secretary Hegseth to distract from his tenure's repeated failings" and "a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters."

"The Trump Administration should reconsider this abhorrent move, which only gives the shooter what he wants: more attention and more control," Reed wrote.

Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., also called on the Pentagon to revoke its decision, saying, "A country cannot condone livestreaming a man's death for entertainment."

"We are long past the days of public hangings in the town square," she wrote on X. "Kids watch what our leaders do and say, is this kind of bloodshed really what we want them seeing?"

entries.title: U.S. working to reverse an Egyptian man's third-country deportation to Africa
entries.summary: The Trump administration's effort to return Ahmed Soliman to the U.S. come after an Arizona judge said his deportation violated due process.
entries.content:
U.S. working to reverse an Egyptian man's third-country deportation to Africa

The Trump administration on Friday said it has started to facilitate the return to the U.S. of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea, in a rare case of the government working to reverse a third-country deportation.

A federal judge in Arizona earlier this week ordered the Department of Homeland Security to return Ahmed Soliman to the U.S. from the country in central Africa where he has no ties, and respond how it plans to do so.

The administration said it is working "collaboratively" with Soliman's lawyers to find and contact him, and is "beginning the process to facilitate" his return, according to Friday's filings in the case from Timothy Courchaine, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona.

Soliman, who is a gay, had been able to get an order from a U.S. immigration judge to prevent him from being deported to his home country, Egypt, where he could be persecuted for his sexuality.

Instead, the Trump administration deported him earlier this year to Equatorial Guinea, which ranks as one of the least free countries in the world, according to Freedom House, a nonprofit devoted to protecting and growing democracy, and human rights across the globe.

Arizona District Court Judge John Hinderaker, an appointee of President Trump, said that DHS violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment when it removed Soliman to a third country.

"It is unrebutted that he has since been held under armed guard; threatened at gunpoint; and arrested, beaten, and held incommunicado by Equatorial Guinean authorities," Hinderaker wrote in his Oct. 6 order.

The ruling comes even as the U.S. Supreme Court last week allowed the Trump administration to resume deportations of migrants to countries where they have no ties, at least for now, while agreeing to take the case up for full oral argument in December.

DHS told NPR in a statement this week that it would comply with lawful court orders and that Soliman would continue to receive due process.

"But the end result will be the same — he will not remain in the U.S. This administration will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson added.

Facilitating Soliman's return

Dana Camilleri, one of Soliman's lawyers, said compliance means diplomats in Equatorial Guinea must work to facilitate Soliman's release. She is working to get a similar outcome for another client in the central African country, a gay Brazilian man.

" We're all just really hopeful that this could be the beginning of getting them home," Camilleri said. "Because they're in an awful situation, and our government put them there."

The office of the U.S. ambassador to Equatorial Guinea did not respond to a request for comment.

Soliman has been held under armed guard at a decommissioned hotel where he has been threatened at gunpoint, arrested, beaten and been unable to communicate with his family or lawyers, according to court filings.

Soliman emigrated to the U.S. from Egypt when he was a child, grew up in Arizona and became a green card holder. He lost his immigration status after a 2023 drug possession and aggravated assault led to a prison sentence.

That's when an immigration judge ruled he could not be sent to Egypt, where he would most likely be tortured.

The harm Soliman is alleged to have suffered in Equatorial Guinea could put the U.S. in violation of international law, according to Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. The council advocates for a fair process for immigrants in the U.S.

" We are signatories of the UN convention against torture, and domestic law makes it illegal to send someone to a place where they will be persecuted," Reichlin-Melnick said. " All of this really violates a lot of the basic principles of due process and human rights that Americans support," and serves as "a direct rebuke to the Trump administration's broader strategy of third country removals."

The Trump administration has made deals with over 30 countries to deport migrants to places where they have no ties or connections as part of the president's immigration crackdown.

Hinderaker's order to return Soliman marks the second time a judge has forced the government to return a third-country migrant from an African nation. A Colorado judge also ordered the return of Brayan Omar Sanchez Servellon, originally from Honduras, who was sent to the Central African Republic earlier this year.

entries.title: Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?
entries.summary: A global treaty signed by 197 countries — including Russia — requires reporting any death that could be a sign of an outbreak to come.
entries.content:
Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?

A 28-year-old woman died in Russia last week and, since then, speculations about the case have ricocheted around the globe.

The woman was a lab technician at a Russian research institute that studies the plague. As unverified rumors have circulated that she may have contracted the disease from a lab leak, President Trump, the World Health Organization and other leaders are asking for more information.

Russia has insisted this is not a health emergency and stated that its health authorities have not found dangerous pathogens in any of the deceased woman's contacts.

But there are still far more questions than answers.

That uncertainty has global leaders and health experts turning to a law that obligates countries, including Russia, to share exactly this type of information. It's called the International Health Regulations or IHR.

On Wednesday, at a WHO press conference, Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus invoked IHR as the best way to determine current situation in Russia and determine the appropriate response.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," he said. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."

Here are the key things to know about the IHR and how it applies in today's world.

Rooted in the 19th century

This law requires countries to share health information that could have international implications. It goes way back to the 1850s with cholera outbreaks in Europe, which led to the creation of guidelines for sharing disease information.

"That's very, very long for international law," says Alexandra Phelan, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "Look at the negotiation documents and they're debating: Is cholera caused by a bacteria or miasma [a bad smell]? Like we're really right in the middle of germ theory."

Then, when WHO was founded in 1948, these regulations — then called the International Sanitary Regulations — were adopted. That was one of the organization's first moves. The law has since been amended and updated, most notably after the SARS or Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome outbreak in 2003 and most recently due to COVID-19 pandemic.

A country is supposed to notify WHO if the health event has the potential to cause an international health emergency.

Today, IHR is among the most widely ratified international treaties, with 197 signatories including the U.S. and Russia. (Even though the Trump administration says it has withdrawn from WHO, the U.S. is still bound by the IHR with the exception of some recent amendments.)

One of the core obligations in the law "is that parties or states must notify WHO within 24 hours of detecting a [serious health] event," explains Phelan.

Some events – like a case of smallpox or a new type of influenza — should immediately trigger a notification. For other situations, a checklist helps a country assess whether notification is needed.

Each year, she says, WHO receives thousands of notifications from all over the world and most turn out to be nothing.

The situation in Russia

Some people fear the Russian woman — who died Oct. 2 — had pneumonic plague. That's one of the diseases "explicitly listed" under IHR, says Phelan, as something to assess and notify the WHO.

However, Russia did not notify WHO about this woman's death. Instead, WHO learned about it through media reports and then, on Oct. 3, went to Russia seeking verification and additional information.

"Russia's response, firstly, was delayed," says Phelan. "But also it wasn't comprehensive."

It took Russia several days to respond. On Oct. 6, health officials told WHO there were no cases of plague in the region and that the woman was hospitalized with severe pneumonia of unknown origin before she died. They also explained that health authorities had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine.

WHO asked Russia for more information, including about lab tests conducted, public health measures and the health status of the woman's contacts. However, as with many international laws, there's no mechanism to make countries comply with the law and share information.

Phelan says the next few days and weeks will be key in understanding how much information Russia is going to share. If they aren't fully transparent, she hopes pressure from other countries either convinces Russia to comply with IHR or, at least, helps keep up the norm of other countries respecting IHR and notifying WHO about future health events.

That kind of notification is critical if the world is to be ready to respond and contain future outbreaks, says Lawrence Gostin, who directs the WHO Center on Global Health Law and is a professor at Georgetown University.

"This case shows the good, the bad and the ugly of the IHR," he says.

"Legally, this is the only thing that's holding Russia to account," Gostin explains. And yet, "you have countries that are hiding the ball."

He believes that the risk to the general population from the current situation in Russia is likely very low. But, for him, the fact that countries can disregard the IHR notification requirements is a "blaring siren about how unprepared we are" to quickly control health threats.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias
entries.summary: Hurricane Isaias is this season's first Atlantic hurricane, and is on a path to hit the northern Gulf Coast. How is the oil industry preparing?
entries.content:
How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias

Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the season, is expected to make landfall on Friday evening near the Alabama Gulf Coast and Florida panhandle.

Days ago, the oil industry around the U.S. Gulf Coast started preparing. A segment of the nation's oil infrastructure — like oil rigs and platforms — operates in the region, although the majority of it is further west, towards western Louisiana and Texas.

Although oil experts are not anticipating major disruptions, oil companies have been taking precautions. Shell and BP have evacuated personnel from offshore facilities close to the storm's path, mainly deepwater platforms. Chevron has evacuated offshore drilling rigs close to the storm's path, and plans to redeploy them once the storm has passed.

In an emailed statement, Exxon told NPR they are "closely monitoring the weather. Operations are normal."

But so far, the storm seems like it will skirt most facilities. The storm's path "could be worse," said Debnil Chowdhury, head of Americas refining at S&P Global Energy. After all, the storm is heading east, and not west, toward where the bulk of oil operations — like refineries — are located.

The storm is "making a swooping turn, almost just to the east of where the most significant infrastructure is," said Bryan Domangue, the Gulf of America region director for the federal Marine Minerals Administration, who oversees offshore oil and natural gas production. "At this point, it's swept just a little south of some of our major deepwater oil and gas facilities, and then it's hugging the eastern boundary of where the infrastructure is."

He added that in addition to evacuating people who work on oil rigs and platforms, which are normal storm precautions, oil operators are doing things like shutting off safety valves below the ocean floor, and moving mobile drilling facilities when possible.

Of course, it's not unprecedented for the oil industry to face hurricanes. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, in 2005, remain some of the most destructive in the oil and gas industry's history. Nearly 3,000 platforms were in the path of the storms and Katrina destroyed 47 platforms. Other, more recent, hurricanes have not been as destructive but have halted production or reduced capacity — such as Hurricane Francine in 2024, Hurricane Ida in 2021, and Hurricane Harvey in 2017.

Another risk is what would happen if the storm became severe enough to make refineries — which are on land — go offline, analysts told NPR. If a hurricane knocks out the power, or if a refinery floods, it can take a while to get running again. It's more complicated than restarting an oil rig or mobile drilling operations.

"Restarting these things is like starting up an old car," said Carl Larry, a manager at Enverus, an energy data and research provider, even if the shutdown is short. "If you did anything in the world, anything in your life, 24/7, stop doing it for one day," he continued, "you're going to have the shakes."

He says, this is because refineries are vast and complex. They boil oil down into molecules that are turned into diesel, gasoline, or natural gas liquids like propane. Pipelines carry crude oil in and refined products out. And they have to be heated. "Every one of those little steps is built on power that's generated through the facility on a constant 24/7 basis," Larry said. If that power is switched off, the process takes time to restart.

There are two significant refineries on the hurricane's path — the Chevron Pascagoula location and the Vertex Alabama refinery. Representatives of these refineries did not return requests for comment about their storm preparations, but Ross Allen, a spokesperson for Chevron, told NPR that generally speaking, refineries prepare for storms by trying to mitigate flood risk.

Chowdhury of S&P Global Energy said these two refineries "account for about 2.5% of total U.S. refining capacity and about 5% the Gulf Coast refining capacity. And Pascagoula specifically is very important to supplying airports throughout the southeast."

While those numbers may not sound big, the global supply of diesel and gas is short, due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. So every little bit counts. American refineries are operating at 92.7% capacity, refining about 17 million barrels of crude a day.

With the midterms weeks away, fuel prices are a sensitive political issue: The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.37 and $6.27 for diesel, according to AAA.

entries.title: Trump says U.S. won't attack Iran before midterms. And, ICE agent shoots man in NYC
entries.summary: Trump announced that the U.S. will not attack Iran ahead of the midterms. And, a 28-year-old man is receiving treatment at the hospital after an ICE agent shot him in the neck.
entries.content:
Bracing For Hurricane Isaias, Ukraine Pushes Russia Back, Iran War Impact On Midterms

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Hurricane Isaias is set to make landfall on the northern Gulf Coast as early as tonight, marking the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. The National Hurricane Center warns of potentially dangerous winds over 100 miles per hour and life-threatening storm surges of five to seven feet. People along the coastlines of Mississippi, Alabama and northwest Florida are preparing for impact.

  • 🎧 Highways are busy with both people fleeing the region and emergency crews deploying to the coast, NPR's Debbie Elliot tells Up First. States are pre-staging personnel and emergency supplies — such as generators, food and water — for distribution during power outages and the cleanup process. Elliot says October feels late for the first hurricane of the season, and that this prominent El Niño weather pattern has led many to believe they have escaped the worst. Forecasters predict serious weather across the southeast, including potential flash flooding and tornadoes. But they say they expect the storm to move through quickly and lose its tropical strength.

Ukraine has launched a new offensive against Russian invaders that employs advanced technology. Operation Vivaldi involves Ukrainian soldiers using electronic warfare and aerial drones to blind Russian reconnaissance and eliminate their firepower and supply routes. They then deploy unmanned land robots to weaken Russian positions. Ukrainians say they have reclaimed around 68 square miles — an area about three times the size of Manhattan.

  • 🎧 This operation is significant because it is unfolding in the Donbas region that Russia has sought to control since 2014, NPR's Joanna Kakissis says. Despite occupying much of the area, Russia demands Ukraine cede the rest in any peace deal, which Ukraine has rejected. Operation Vivaldi demonstrates that a complete Russian takeover of Donbas is not inevitable, and Ukrainian forces can still achieve breakthroughs in a battlefield dense with drones, Kakissis says. Russia continues its attacks on Ukrainian cities, especially in the east. A recent strike on a public bus in Kramatorsk, one of the last Ukrainian-held cities, killed at least 30 people and injured many others, according to local authorities.

President Trump announced on social media that the U.S. will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on Nov. 3. He is aiming to counter reports suggesting the White House is considering airstrikes against Iran before election day.

  • 🎧 Trump's announcement is a bit surprising because ideally, he wouldn't want to make those kinds of promises during a war, NPR's Domenico Montanaro says. He adds that the president's post signals his awareness that the conflict has been politically bad for his party ahead of elections. More strikes and deeper involvement in the conflict are a tough sell to the American public, including his own base. Despite promising to avoid foreign entanglements, Trump has argued that the prolonged, unpopular war is necessary to prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon.

At least one U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer fired seven rounds during an immigration enforcement operation in New York City yesterday. The officer struck a 28-year-old immigrant from the Dominican Republic in the neck, according to NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch. The man, identified by Tisch as Oscar Belgal, was shot below his left ear and arrived at NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital in stable condition. A 5-year-old boy, believed to be Belgal's son, was inside Belgal's vehicle during the incident. Police later located the child safe and in the care of a family member. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed that Belgal was the target of the operation, but did not explain why the officer fired his weapon. (via Gothamist)

Today's listen

An amateur Philadelphia-based a cappella group filled with suburban dads and grandfathers is taking social media by storm with their style and vocal arrangements. The Tonics are nearing 100,000 Instagram followers, up from 500 last year. Their rise is largely due to Emilie Hagen, a millennial influencer and "comedic journalist," who promoted their videos to her 130,000 followers. Hagen tells NPR she believes the group resonates with audiences because they feel authentic and wholesome, and they showcase a different side of how men interact beyond activities like sports. Listen to The Tonics sing and read more about why they are gaining such a following.

Weekend picks

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Oscar-winning documentarian Alex Gibney spent four years researching tech billionaire Elon Musk by reviewing extensive documents and interviewing people close to him. The nearly four-hour film, Musk, is in theaters today ahead of its HBO release.

📺 TV: Netflix's East of Eden, starring Florence Pugh, offers an epic retelling of an American classic that provides a fresh perspective, Pop Culture Happy Hour says.

📚 Books: It's time to say goodbye to beach reads and welcome cozy autumn books. NPR's Book of the Day host Andrew Limbong shares 10 exciting books coming this fall, featuring titles from Barbara Kingsolver, Chad Harbach, Jasmine Guillory and more.

🎵 Music: Troye Sivan's She's The Best explores darker feelings with a mix of gloom and bright, bombastic moments, all while continuing to honor the legacy of queer dance floors in his music videos, NPR Music's Isabella Gomez Sarmiento says.

🎭 Theater: In the Broadway play School Girls; or, the African Mean Girls Play, the ladies at Aburi Girls' Boarding School navigate difficult lessons through their friendships, conflicts and the upcoming Miss Ghana 1986 beauty pageant. Playwright Jocelyn Bioh and director Whitney White join It's Been A Minute host Brittany Luse to discuss the story's significance.

❓ Quiz: This week's quiz will test your knowledge on protests, Nobels and even a K-pop superstar. While I may not have a prize for you upon completion, I can provide a hint: at least two of the answers were featured in the "Today's top stories" section of this newsletter this week.

3 things to know before you go

  • The Norwegian Nobel Committee has awarded this year's Nobel Peace Prize to human rights lawyer Navanethem "Navi" Pillay. Pillay, who has served as the U.N. human rights chief and a judge on the International Court of Justice, was recognized for her contributions to international justice.
  • Three astronauts and a cosmonaut from NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission have returned to Earth after an almost eight-month trip to the International Space Station, where they conducted spacewalks, science experiments and research.
  • New research reveals surprising similarities in the gut microbiomes of Tanzanian hunter-gatherers and Bolivian horticulturalists, suggesting that their microbial kinship dates back long before human migration separated their ancestors.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: Why American investors love European defense startups
entries.summary: As European defense spending takes off, just about half of the funding in Europe's defense tech industry is coming from American investors this year. One reason why: European investment firms have restrictions on how they can invest.
entries.content:
Why American investors love European defense startups

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

Have you ever wondered what Warren Buffett does in his free time? Turns out he's a YouTube guy, as prone to the rabbit hole as any of us. You might expect the recently retired Berkshire Hathaway CEO to consume nerdy financial content, but no. According to The Wall Street Journal, we learned he's prone to watching Paul Anka videos, clips of Bill Murray films, and my personal favorite … O'zbekiston Got Talent, the Uzbek knock-off of America's Got Talent. But who hasn't gone through that phase?

Coming up

  • European defense start-ups are raking in cash; Americans are benefiting
  • These six power plants should be offline. This is what they cost tax-payers
  • Why Florida college enrollment seems to be doing well

Trivia: What do most countries with a sovereign wealth fund have in common? Email your answer to indicator@npr.org

News We're Watching

Why U.S. investors are throwing money at defense start-ups - Bloomberg

What to Know: American investors are seeing an opportunity in Europe. The continent saw a 14 percent rise in military spending to $864 billion last year, due to pressure from Russia and Trump's own unhappiness with low spending from NATO allies. The hike is prompting a spate of new defense start-ups keeping up with modern warfare. They're building tech like AI-powered battlefield management, drones, and spy satellites. These start-ups are already bidding and winning contracts… so the pay-off is coming fast. In fact, these startups have raised a RECORD amount of capital this year, with help from Americans.

Why the U.S. is loving this: Just about half of the funding in Europe's defense tech industry is coming from American investors this year! What's up?

  • European VC's aren't remotely measuring up: Europe does have venture capital (VC) firms. But there's about €150 billion in EU-based funds versus more than a trillion dollars in its U.S. counterparts. U.S. firms are out-investing EU ones at every funding round level, getting significantly larger at later-stage rounds when the big, risky checks are needed.
  • American investors are seeing dollar signs: NATO allies have committed to investing 5% of GDP into defense. That means a lot of government contracts. Cody Huggins, a partner at Scout Ventures, a VC firm, told CNBC last year, "you're going to see high-caliber entrepreneurs that otherwise wouldn't have built in this space because they would be concerned that there weren't the contracts or the venture capital or growth equity in Europe."
  • Restrictions on European investment: Some European money comes with restrictions on defense spending. For example, the European Investment Bank limits investment in weapons and ammo for ethical reasons. The German fund KfW Capital won't finance what it deems 'controversial' weapons.

These power plants should be offline. Whose paying to keep them going? - E & E News

What to Know: Five coal-fired power plants and one running on oil and gas would no longer be online if not for the Trump administration. The Department of Energy used emergency authority to keep the plants going past their scheduled retirement, something that's never been done in the history of the DOE. It was also against the wishes of some of the plants. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said it's about giving people access to more reliable power to help address periods of peak demand. What's odd: several of the plants are running at limited capacity or not at all. That said, utilities are still incurring millions of dollars just to maintain a power plant on standby. Wright told Reuters last year that he expects most of the nation's power plants to hold off on retirement in order to help power artificial intelligence aka data centers.

Why it matters: Electricity costs nationwide are already wildly high as demand increases from AI. Consumers Energy, the company that owns the Michigan J.H. Campbell coal plant, reported to the SEC that the plant has cost them $259 million to continue running since May of last year. The utility has gone to its customers to pay for $138 million of that cost. A recent court decision also found the 'emergency' order was an overstep and threatened the stability of the energy market.

Emergency orders are keeping a generating unit at a coal-fired plant in Colorado going as well. The latest happened Sept. 27. The DOE has to keep issuing them within 90 days. Keeping that plant online would cost taxpayers $80 million annually, according to its Governor. That's without it producing basically any power.

Our question on the team: What does this mean for other energy developers? Does the regulatory uncertainty affect new investment given the continued 90-day renewals?

Update: President Trump looks to lower diesel costs - NPR

Last week, we spoke in the newsletter about why diesel costs tend to be higher than regular gas. Diesel prices have hit a record high in the past month, and the Trump administration had considered an export ban to try and lower prices. Well now, the administration has made its move. No export ban! BUT… President Trump issued an executive order to defer the payment of a 24 cent excise tax on diesel for on-highway driving through the end of the year.

Today's Indicator

The awkward art of asking friends to pay you back

If you HAVEN'T listened: If you've ever used 'Venmo' as a verb, you likely know the pain of someone not paying you back. You generously offered your credit card to pay for dinner, your co-diner promised to pay you back, you send a Venmo request and *deflating balloon sound*... they don't do it. A day goes by, TWO. Venmo tells us about 40% of people take a week or MORE to settle debts with friends. Transferring money may be easy, but getting that money back? Less so.

In the full episode, we hear first-hand accounts from listeners on THEIR Venmo experiences.

If you HAVE listened: The reporter Ricky Mulvey tells us that we didn't have time to get into all the reasons why someone doesn't get paid back on Venmo. A few remaining:

  • A Venmo request gets buried in a string of other notifications. The person who owes money simply forgets.
  • The person who is owed money is trying to "optimize". This can happen if you are the person who wants to put your card down at a group dinner. You get the credit card points, but now you've got several people, including some folks you may not know owing you money.
  • Not understanding someone else's financial situation. This comes from being the inclusive friend. You want to include everyone on a big trip, but may not fully realize the financial burden it could put on someone.

The most salient advice from the episode is that a Venmo is a personal loan. And if you give out a personal loan, the money may not come back to you.

Rest of the Week

Why Norway's sovereign wealth fund is facing its own Ed Sheeran moment

How increased ICE raids impact hospitals

Listener Mailbag

Listener Mia Calle is messaging from Port St. Lucie, Fl.

Question: My name is Mia, and I am a high school math teacher in Florida and mother of two young daughters. I keep hearing about how it is becoming increasingly difficult for students to be admitted to colleges in Florida from my colleagues.

Can you help me reconcile the decline in college enrollment nationally with the increase in competition to enroll in public universities in Florida? Is the latter because the state has the Bright Futures program which is based on merit and may encourage a wider pool of applicants compared to other states? I grew up in Michigan after the Michigan (broken) Promise Scholarship fell through. Are there other states that offer similar programs? Is this an antidote to reverse the national downward trend in college enrollment?

Answer: Just last week, we were talking on the show how college enrollment is set to decline steadily through 2041. Florida has seen college enrollment steadily rise the past three years and is set to do the same into next year. We don't know whether the trend will continue… BUT we do know the South is set to keep churning out high school graduates at a steady pace. Tennessee is set to see a 15 percent bump by 2041, South Carolina 14 percent and… Florida at a 12 percent increase! 

Here are some potential contributing factors to Florida's college enrollment increasing the past few years:

  • Price: Florida has the MOST affordable in-state tuition and fees, according to U.S. News & World Report. The website has also ranked Florida the NUMBER ONE state for higher education for the past 11 years.
  • Demand from out-of-state students: In 2021-2022, Florida had the 11th-lowest OUT-of-state tuition. AND both the University of Florida and Florida State University are among the most affordable highly rated schools for out-of-state tuition.
  • Bright Futures: This is a scholarship program to help high-achieving Florida high school grads afford school in-state. Last year, in the 2024-25 school year, 37,114 new students got disbursements to help pay for school in-state.

You said you kept hearing how Florida schools are becoming more competitive. Well, at least for the University of Florida, its acceptance rate IS certainly getting tougher. From ~33% a few years ago to 19.8% last year. It's made quite a few top college lists which helps this competitiveness too.

Thanks for your question, Mia!If you have an economics question, send us a message at indicator@npr.org.

In Our Spare Time

Co-host Adrian Ma is watching PBS Newshour

I've been watching a lot of PBS NewsHour lately, which is funny to me, because for the longest time, I wasn't a TV-news person.

I grew up in a Fox News household. Ever since it went on the air in the 90s, there was always a TV in my house turned to O'Reilly, Beck, Hannity or Ingraham. And that shaped my idea of TV news: shouty hosts, flashy sets, woosh-y graphics, and sensational headlines. It wasn't for me, but it certainly wasn't boring. TV that gets your fight-or-flight response going. Because of that, I avoided watching TV news for many years.

Then a few years ago, I started watching PBS NewsHour. At first, I thought, "This is BORING TV." But the more I watched, the more I came to see its boringness as a superpower. It delivers the news in a way that's smart, respectful, non-sensational, calm, and humane. In short, it is boring in the best way.

entries.title: Why mailing a ballot close to Election Day may get it rejected for a late postmark
entries.summary: If you're using the U.S. Postal Service to return a ballot close to Election Day, officials recommend getting it postmarked at a post office to avoid getting caught up in mail processing changes.
entries.content:
Why mailing a ballot close to Election Day may get it rejected for a late postmark

Relying on the U.S. Postal Service to return a mail-in ballot close to Election Day now comes with an additional risk for many voters — a late postmark that gets a vote rejected.

The risk stems from mailing system changes that began last year. And those changes have pushed some election officials to encourage voters to consider returning their ballots at their local election office or any available drop boxes instead.

The calls to avoid mailboxes also come as trust in the Postal Service delivering mail ballots on time has fallen, and after President Trump pushed to restrict voting by mail for the midterm elections but was blocked by the Supreme Court.

Election officials often use the date of the postmark that USPS stamps on envelopes to determine whether a ballot was sent by Election Day.

About a week before next month's Election Day, USPS says it plans to roll out special postmarking procedures at post offices affected by the changes as part of its "extraordinary measures" policy to boost mail service for federal general elections.

Still, the agency continues to recommend that voters mail back ballots at least a week before their state's deadline. And in states with a grace period for receiving late-arriving mail ballots, USPS recommends stopping by a post office to ask for a manual postmark to make sure a ballot gets postmarked on the same day it's mailed.

How mailing system changes led to the risk of late postmarks

Since April 2025, USPS has been rolling out cuts to daily mail pick-ups and processing changes at certain post offices, especially in rural areas. What USPS calls its "Regional Transportation Optimization" effort is part of a 10-year reorganization plan the agency began in 2021 to try to stabilize its finances.

As a result, USPS may not automatically stamp a date on an envelope the same day it's collected by a letter carrier or dropped off at a post office or a big blue collection box.

As part of its "extraordinary measures" for these midterms, USPS has instructed post offices affected by RTO to separate returned ballots from other mail starting Oct. 26 so that managers can manually add postmarks the day the ballots are collected.

That procedure was not in place during this year's primary elections, which saw increased ballot rejection rates in multiple states.

Elena Patel, a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, says she is encouraged by the steps USPS plans to take in the coming weeks to address concerns about late postmarks.

But the situation is still risky for voters, Patel adds, given that it's not clear how post offices will carry out these directives for the first time, particularly in places where staffing may be stretched.

For the general election, an additional 43,000 to 55,000 ballots around the country could be rejected for arriving late because of the RTO effort, according to a new analysis by Patel, who produced the estimates before USPS announced its final extraordinary measures policy.

"These are some of the realities of running a very large postal network on tight finances," says Patel, who once worked as an economist at the Postal Regulatory Commission.

USPS plans to take other "extraordinary measures" for mail-in ballots

USPS has outlined other extraordinary measures:

  • Starting Oct. 24, 10 days before Election Day, some post offices may extend their opening and closing times by a half-hour and set up lines or drive-through lanes just for voters who want to get a manual postmark for their mail-in ballot.
  • And starting Oct. 26, USPS says it plans to speed up delivery of ballots.

Asked why it is not starting extraordinary measures 15 days before Election Day, as it did for the 2024 and 2022 elections, USPS said in a statement: "The time period for extraordinary measures is carefully considered in advance of each General Election, and it is based on a number of internal factors. The Postal Service has successfully delivered America's election mail for more than 150 years, and we are confident that we will do so again this year."

Still, some eligible voters who rely on voting by mail are between "a rock and a hard place" when trying to navigate the mailing system, says Michelle Sparck, director of Get Out the Native Vote, a voter education organization in Alaska.

No post offices in the state are affected by the RTO effort, but Sparck, a member of the Qissunamiut Tribe of Chevak, says she has come across many absentee voters in Alaska Native villages who had their ballots rejected — an outcome that she fears will discourage some from trying to vote again.

"The No. 1 reason for that was postmarking delays. Now, even on a good Alaskan day with no weather challenges, it doesn't mean we're going to have an operational post office on a business day during business hours," Sparck says. "It's always, always easier said than done to kind of go along with the system's rules. But the system doesn't exactly work for us."

For now, Sparck is encouraging eligible voters to make a plan to be an October voter and not wait until November's Election Day if they can.

"If there is an early voting opportunity in a community," Sparck says, "we're asking people to drop their ballots off with those folks so that it becomes part of the chain of custody."

Edited by Benjamin Swasey
